idiom_name: trait-bounded type parameter on the host (monomorphized static dispatch)
implementation_notes: Rust expresses policies natively: the host is generic over a policy type with a trait bound (struct Cache<K, V, P: EvictionPolicy<K>> { ... }), the trait states the contract the compiler enforces where the policy is bound, and monomorphization makes the calls static and inlinable - the property the C++ idiom exists for, without duck typing or template-template parameters. The standard library itself exposes policy parameters this way (HashMap<K, V, S = RandomState> where S: BuildHasher, and Vec<T, A: Allocator> with the allocator trait), including associated types for further policy-chosen types such as BuildHasher::Hasher. When the policy must be chosen after creation, use a dyn Trait object at the boundary instead of adding a generic parameter.
pitfalls: Monomorphization duplicates code per policy type: generous generic policies grow binary size and compile times, and hosts with different policies cannot share a collection (use dyn at the boundary if they must).

A bound placed on the host's impl block restricts every method; put `where` clauses on the methods that need them so policies are not over-constrained (a Clone bound, say, would rule out lock-holding policies).
The orphan rule prevents a downstream crate from implementing a policy trait for a foreign type: design policy traits so users can wrap their type (newtype) instead of implementing for it.
